Research problem: MVFA's few-shot mode fine-tunes the adapters on K normal plus K abnormal target images with pixel masks; can this labelled support set be replaced by an unlabelled pool of target scans? We ask whether source-free self-training of the segmentation and detection adapters on pseudo-labels from MVFA's own zero-shot maps — where a pixel is pseudo-labelled only if all four feature levels agree (it lies in the lowest or highest 10% of scores at every level) and all other pixels are ignored — improves image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on a disjoint test split of the target modality, and how many unlabelled scans N are needed to match few-shot MVFA with K = 4 labelled normal and abnormal images. Each target dataset is split 50/50 (by patient where identifiers exist) into the unlabelled pool and the test set.
Rationale: The corrected limitation G4 shows that MVFA's 'K-shot' setting requires 2K annotated target images including masks, while clinical reality at a new site is usually a large unlabelled archive and no annotation budget. Pseudo-label adaptation exists for CLIP-based localisation (AnoCLIP's test-time adaptation), but not for multi-level medical adapters under modality shift, where wrong pseudo-labels can reinforce errors. Agreement across MVFA's four levels is a confidence signal specific to its design, and the number of unlabelled scans needed to match K labelled pairs is a directly actionable answer. This differs from training with image-level labels on the source (the other problem of this group) because the target here has no labels at all. It is implementable with the existing training loop and mask-based losses restricted to confident pixels, and runs on one GPU.

Feedback: Argue why cross-level agreement should be more reliable than single-level confidence under modality shift, and test it.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G3. Localisation supervision requires dense masks: MVFA trains two branches. The detection (classification) adapters receive an image-level BCE loss on every source image, including the three BMAD datasets that have no masks (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS). The segmentation adapters, which produce the anomaly maps, are trained only with Dice and Focal losses on pixel-level masks, i.e. only on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. Localisation therefore depends entirely on dense expert masks from three datasets; no image-level, sparse or normal-only supervision of the segmentation branch is formulated.
- G4. The few-shot setting needs labelled abnormal images with masks and is evaluated on one draw: In the released code, 'K-shot' means K normal AND K abnormal images, the abnormal ones with pixel masks, both drawn from BMAD's valid/ split; the adapters are fine-tuned on them per target task. Clinical few-shot supervision may instead contain only normal or unlabelled images, which the method does not support. Only one fixed draw per dataset is provided. Training time and compute for the per-task fine-tuning are not reported.

Problem: Is agreement across MVFA's four feature levels a reliable confidence signal for source-free adaptation to a new modality? Starting from source-trained MVFA, we pseudo-label pixels of an unlabelled target pool only where all four levels' zero-shot maps agree (lowest or highest 10% at every level), fine-tune both segmentation and detection adapters for three self-training rounds with losses restricted to those pixels, and compare against single-level (deepest-layer) confidence with the same pixel budget. Outcomes on a disjoint 50/50 test split: image AUROC, pixel AUROC and PRO versus unlabelled pool size N; the precision of the pseudo-labels against ground-truth masks; and the N at which performance matches few-shot MVFA with K = 4 labelled normal and abnormal images.

Rationale: Reviewers asked why cross-level agreement should be better than single-level confidence, for the self-training schedule, and for failure analysis. The problem is now centred on that comparison, measures pseudo-label precision directly, and fixes three rounds with both adapter sets updated. The deployment decision (how many unlabelled scans replace K labelled pairs) remains the practical outcome.
